title: Assume Form
content:
Emily Nola is a curator, writer, and researcher based in upstate New York.

Do Not Research does not, has not, and will never exist:

Assume Form
April 4 – May 24, 2026
Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College

Curated by: Emily Nola
Artist/Participants: Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, Lendl Barcelos, Oneohtrix Point Never, 0rphan Drift, Sadie Plant

In 1995, the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) was formed at the University of Warwick in England. Initiated within the Department of Philosophy by theorist and research fellow Sadie Plant, the unit produced a collectively authored body of work that straddled theory and fiction. The collective and its collaborators operated on the fringes of academia, drawing on a wide range of influences including continental philosophy, science fiction, and electronic music. Moving across forms both native and unique to the philosophical discipline including essays, zines, performances, and events, their work attempted to expand the limits of theoretical production. At the advent of the World Wide Web, amidst a present and future unsettled by emergent technologies, they turned to the speculative to interpret these new terrains.

A wide range of figures emerge from the CCRU’s annals. It is this mixed legacy of various influential, maligned, and underexplored practices that led to the uneven dissemination of the milieu’s output via the very platform they grappled with: the internet. There, their legacy is distorted, co-opted by obscure online political sects and Silicon Valley accelerationists.

Assume Form attempts to reconstruct what alchemized within the unit. Via the various influences and practices that entered their orbit, it reimagines this defining chapter of technological and cultural history. The exhibition frames the CCRU as the crystallization of its historical moment, tracking the landscape in which they operated from 1994 until the turn of the millennium. Taking cues from the same sources as the group——the landscapes, texts, sounds, and events that informed them and them——it creates the imagined space in which the ongoing resonances of this highly influential group begin assuming form.

0rphan Drift is an artist collective and avatar, formed in London in 1994. It is currently channeled through the artists Maggie Roberts and Ranu Mukherjee and previously was transmitted through many others including Suzanne Karakashian and Erle Stenberg. Its work, via video, performance, collage, text, and installation, explores a rapidly changing technological landscape and the implications of that landscape on both the human and the machinic body. This conversation took place in February 2026, on the occasion of the exhibition Assume Form, which is on view until May 24th at the Hessel Museum at Bard College. It has been edited for length and clarity.

Emily Nola (EN): Tell me about the beginning of 0rphan Drift. Where were you? What was the environment?

Maggie Roberts (MR): The project started when we were both teaching at Middlesex University in London. The other two members of 0rphan Drift in the ’90s and early 2000s, Suzanne Karakashian and Erle Stenberg, were both students there. We were all sort of searching for what to do next. We didn’t feel we had a place in the YBA [Young British Artists], goal-oriented, career art scene. We wanted to do something different.

Ranu Mukherjee (RM): I remember having conversations during my MFA where I was trying to talk about the feeling that everything was going to change because of the internet—which was just starting. And the response from some faculty was: Why aren’t you painting? Why are you talking about this? It was treated like an improper subject.

London was between gentrifications, and there were tons of empty spaces. We were offered a space on Underwood Street, and Maggie had been offered a show at Cabinet Gallery. She got back from a trip, and I remember saying, “I think we should just make a show that doesn’t have authorship, that is collectively made.” And you said, “I think my Cabinet show is going to be that, and I’ve been thinking about this word ‘orphan.’” So Maggie unpackaged that solo show and made it into this collective thing.

MR: Solo career wrecked!

RM: It was the beginning of sampling culture, too. We took that very seriously. The Cyberpositive book (1995) was sampled, as well as the photos from that first exhibition, and alot of the work at Underwood Street.1 That was a little different, but it was also reconfigurations of material and object.

MR: It’s pretty fun to talk about that piece—that’s Ariadne’s Gone Virtual (1995).

EN: I’ve been thinking a lot about that show. It’s one of my favorites from that early time. There’s a line in that text that reads: “Your identity must become mutable and hyperaware. Navigation through response.” When I talk about 0rphan Drift, I often talk about it as a feminist collective. It’s interesting that this show—which is oriented around the mythological figure Ariadne, this lineage of feminism—in the first or second sentence, there’s an unseating of that. How do you both think about this project in relation to feminism, or cyberfeminism—a term that had just been coined around that time? Did you think of this project as a feminist one?

RM: The influence was definitely there. At the end of my MFA, I found Donna Haraway’s “A Cyborg Manifesto,” and I was like, this is the missing piece. The white feminism that was “goddess” oriented felt problematic. Donna Haraway really broke that up for me. The Ariadne work was a way of putting that figure into a cyberfeminist context. I don’t know if we used that term then, but we were painting with that brush.

MR: For me, feminism—or, dismantling patriarchal assumptions—was definitely something I was thinking about. But I was thinking it through different kinds of temporalities and materialities, thinking in a way that is labyrinthine and fluid, and refuses to be fixed. It’s amazing, Ranu—I didn’t realize you had just read Haraway. That’s insane. That’s so contemporary of you. I think I was obsessed with [the novelist and filmmaker] Marguerite Duras and [the filmmaker] Andrei Tarkovsky.

RM: I mean, they were definitely there for me, too. And [filmmaker and theorist] Trinh T. Minh-ha … But the “earthy” feminisms felt really predatory to me. They were just picking things out of other cultures, some of which my family are part of. They took so much from that history and it bugged me; I couldn’t align with that. Cyberfeminism was a way of getting out of that grip.

EN: Most of the work being shown in Assume Form was also part of Syzygy (1999), your collaboration with the CCRU [Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, held at Beaconsfield Contemporary Art, London]. That was your only formal collaboration with them, but you were in conversation for much of the late ’90s. Can you tell me a little bit about how you first got involved with them, what that collaboration looked like?

MR: I first met [philosopher] Nick Land when he spoke at the Royal College of Art in London in 1992. He talked about science fiction and William Gibson’s novel Neuromancer (1984), and I felt the way Ranu did about Haraway. Not about Nick, but about what I was being introduced to. Well, his thinking then as well, actually—but mostly the science-fiction space, how it was articulating incredible stuff: How it acted as a tool for rupture and recoding. So that was my introduction, and he also financially supported the Cyberpositive book.

RM: In those early days of 0rphan Drift, besides exhibiting, we were also working in clubs, doing visuals for music and performance lectures at institutions. They invited us to perform at Virtual Futures, which got us connected to that whole burgeoning thought bubble.2

MR: VNS Matrix stands out for me.

RM: Yeah, and Hari Kunzru was there, and Pat Cadigan, a big spectrum of people …

MR: Stelarc, Manuel DeLanda, and Sadie Plant, who was backing off a bit by that time … She did amazing talks around [what would become her book] Zeros and Ones (1997).3 Also, I think we did some sort of backing visuals and vocals for some Nick thing.

EN: For Meltdown (1994), right?4

MR: Meltdown, that’ll be it. But it was a slow burn—just staying in touch, lots of respect and mutual exploration. It took us a year to write the proposal for Syzygy. We were all into aspects of Mayan calendrics, but some of our other interests diverged. They were brilliant together, but if anyone asks me about the Numogram, I don’t know what to say—fourth-dimensional math is just not my thing, you know?

RM: The CCRU were numerology and mathematics based; we were interested in qualitative stuff that was based on cosmology. It feels to me like when we moved into production, the Numogram, hyperstition, and the different narratives that they came up with got really fleshed out for them, whereas we really fleshed out the video and the avatars.

MR: [CCRU members] Nick, Anna Greenspan, and Mark Fisher went to a hut in a forest in Canada to write. We, 0rphan Drift, were making the collages, videos, and soundtracks, and Steve Goodman [a.k.a. Kode9, a music producer and member of the CCRU] collaborated with us on sound. Suzanne Karakashian and [CCRU member] Suzanne Livingston made the icons for the twinnings together. And the Meshed Katacomic publication (1999)—which we were very excited about—we worked on all together. That was a disaster for CCRU, because it was illegible for them. We’re so used to reading fast-moving, disrupted video. So that’s what brought about the Abstract Culture: Digital Hyperstition pamphlet (1999), actually.5 There was a bit of extra money, so they used it to publish that. That’s what I remember. But what about you, Ranu?

RM: That’s right, because CCRU wanted more text in the Katacomic. It was based on the idea of a comic book or graphic novel, so having full pages of theoretical texts wasn’t right for the format. Part of it was also that their narrative was not ours. They had all this … very Lovecraft-inflected Cthulhu narrative, and we weren’t doing that. By the end of the project—which was interesting, because it was called Syzygy, and we really brought that on—by the end I felt like we were in this cosmological battle or something. I don’t know if we could adopt all of it—also I don’t think we understood all of it. I didn’t feel compelled to go in that direction.

EN: Yeah, it’s interesting, I think you both are alighting on what I’ve found through researching that period. Late ’98 to 2000 is a transition point for the CCRU. They move operations from the University of Warwick campus to Leamington Spa, and Sadie Plant’s initial influence starts dissipating. That’s when the Lovecraftian, occultic, conspiratorial thinking hits a fever pitch, and the work really changes.

MR: At that time, there was just this darkness around. Suzanne and I got a lot of inspiration for patterns and textures and footage for the videos from going to squat parties, and that went from being an amazing experience—obviously, it involved psychedelics—to all the sudden, people injecting and overdosing and dying. Suddenly, there was so much more heaviness present in London.

EN: Over the process of working on the show together, I’ve become curious as to what it’s been like to go back and spend time with this period of your life, of the collective’s life. What has it been like to look back? Or, does it even feel new?

MR: No, it doesn’t. I was saying to Ranu the other day: Why does everyone want our old work? There’s also this assumption that we “illustrated” the CCRU—an assumption made mostly by men of a certain age group. They keep writing to me, and they’ll say something that I just can’t stand, like—“Just one more question, did Nick Land write Cyberpositive?” I just kind of end up telling them to get lost. That’s not been great, and I’ve fielded a lot of that.

RM: Being in San Francisco and watching the tech stuff has been really disturbing. And I’ve had to reckon with—did we miss something that was coming? The word accelerationism wasn’t being used when we were part of this, and people don’t really understand that. Watching it all unfold right in front of my face was really … we’re still in it right now, and there’s another wave coming. It depends on which way AI goes and how AGI [artificial general intelligence] unfolds—but that debate is very close. It feels very close … I mean, anyone who’s aligned with Nick’s work now is a conspirator in desiring the full domination of AI over humans, over all life.

You know? That’s actually what some of the tech community is trying to do. It’s not even hidden anymore.6

EN: Well back then, in the ’90s, you hear Meltdown, you know, it’s fun, it’s cyberpunky. It’s science fiction about a speculative future. But now, that future is really coming to pass. So to continue to take it on as, like, an ideological rallying cry means something really different today than it did in 1994.

RM: Totally! You’re not standing outside politics. You’re directly influencing it now.

MR: But I think, Ranu, when you’re saying, “Did we miss something?” I don’t think we did. I have thought about this a lot. Back when Nick was writing Meltdown, I loved his word-crafting. Not that I understood everything, but I kind of don’t mind that. And then I heard slowly, incrementally, what he’d been doing [in the intervening years]. I suppose, to begin with, I thought: He’s always prescient. He moved to Shanghai because he was already talking about the rise of China, when no one else was thinking that was the future. There’s so much stuff that he was prescient about, and that sat alongside his Nietzschean-Bataillian nihilism okay for a bit. But then I suddenly started getting these little inklings of … he’s homophobic, he’s misogynist, he’s damning the entire Global South to disease and starvation. And I didn’t know what to make of any of it.

And that’s when I was asked to do an artist talk at Goldsmiths, at the University of London. I got asked whether I had publicly disowned Nick Land. And I said, no, I hadn’t. It was so extreme, and no one had a good plan. But out of all this has emerged Donald Trump, and it’s serious.

EN: Yeah, I mean you’re right, it is serious. But also, I think—I believe strongly that—to just disown and essentially cease to engage is also not the right answer. You know? To pretend like it’s not happening, or that it didn’t happen—it’s how we got to this point. So doing that clearly doesn’t work, and we need to find a different strategy than total disassociation and disengagement.

With all of the ambivalence that we’ve just talked about, it feels like the easiest option would be to not engage this history, not talk about this period of the work. I’m thinking specifically in the context of bringing it into Assume Form, into a new exhibition for current audiences—I’m curious, both personally and in a larger sense, why it feels like dealing with these histories is still important?

MR: We think about 0rphan Drift as an avatar: It’s a strange attractor that we channel. That feels real, still today. So I’ve decided that, instead of feeling frustrated, it’s about understanding 0rphan Drift as a continuum. We’re figuring out how we want to move forward in the current moment.

RM: It’s a story that’s not fully told. And the spectrum of possibilities when the computational technology first arrived was very multivalent. There was a lot of hopefulness and potential, as well as fear. We’re in another moment like that. I think our work was asking certain questions, and they are a part of an important conversation to continue to have. It’s also frustrating to not be able to talk about the work as it was. We were living in the moment, even though we were thinking about the future—because the future felt like it was happening in that moment. I think some of the ideas are still really important, but the work has not yet been fully understood. If the legacy of that time is just Nick Land and the CCRU, it’s very incomplete.

Originally published in the publication for Assume Form, designed by Eric Timothy Carlson. The exhibition is on view at the Hessel Museum at Bard College from April 4 - May 24, 2026. Find more information here.

1

Cyberpositive is an experimental science-fiction novel published by 0rphan Drift in 1995. An earlier version was released as a catalogue to accompany their inaugural exhibition at Cabinet Gallery, 0(rphan>)d>rift (1994).

2

The Virtual Futures conferences were held at the University of Warwick annually from 1994 to 1996. They explored cyberculture across a range of disciplines including art, philosophy, and science.

3

Participants of the 1995 Virtual Futures conference mentioned here include the cyberfeminist artist collective VNS Matrix, writer Hari Kunzru (at the time, a student at Warwick), cyberpunk novelist Pat Cadigan, performance artist Stelarc, theorist Manuel DeLanda, and theorist and founder of the CCRU, Sadie Plant.

4

Nick Land’s Meltdown is a lecture-performance first given at the Virtual Futures conference in 1994. It was later included as a cassette tape with the first edition of the zine ****collapse (1994) and published as text in the CCRU’s pamphlet series Abstract Culture (1997). It currently circulates in many versions online, some of which incorrectly claim affiliation with 0rphan Drift and use their more recent work without permission.

5

Abstract Culture is a series of pamphlets published by the CCRU in four collections (called swarms) between 1997 and 1999. While very few physical copies of the pamphlets exist (the Assume Formexhibition includes reproductions), the texts included are available on the CCRU’s website www.ccru.net.

6

Since the dissolution of the CCRU, Land’s work has become explicitly aligned with far-right reactionary thinkers and ideologies. His work has particular influence in Silicon Valley, where it is taken up by influential tech executives to justify anti-humanist impulses.
author: Do Not Research
